column3: Contrasts divine non-wronging with people wronging themselves, while also distributing people into repeated groups.
Joins the revealed Book, divinely given plurality, and the command to race in good deeds.
Directly parallels Allah's choosing, though it concerns selected prophetic houses rather than heirs of the Book.
Its differentiated messengers and repeated group division give only a broad structural parallel.
The immediately preceding verse identifies the revealed Book as truth and grounds the inheritance statement.
Uses self-wronging in a garden account, but not the Book's heirs or their graded response.
Directly names the moderate person, though in the distinct setting of fidelity after deliverance at sea.
The nearby declaration of human succession complements the focus's language of inherited stewardship.
Names an oppressive people, offering a public counterpart to the focus's self-wronging heir.
Divides communities between divine guidance and settled error, echoing differentiated responses among people.
Its warning that apparent good may harm the self is a limited counterpart to self-wronging.
Uses precedence in good as a contested social measure, unlike the focus's divinely enabled precedence.
The shared description of faithful servants is too general to clarify selection or inheritance.
Divine preservation of heaven and earth does not materially develop the focus's human inheritance theme.
Calls successful believers inheritors, but leaves the inherited object and recipient gradation unspecified.
Commands a race toward forgiveness and calls it Allah's great bounty, closely matching precedence and bounty.
Shows the Qur'an benefiting believers while increasing wrongdoers in loss, a clear differentiated reception of the Book.
Allah's permission limits harm, but the setting does not concern delegated good works or inheritance.
The shared description of faithful servants is too general to clarify selection or inheritance.
Links a claimed book-based proof with wrongdoers' deception, providing a nearby contrast to true book inheritance.
Explicitly denies divine wrongdoing and attributes consequence to human deeds, illuminating self-wronging.
Describes revelation as a Book and guiding light given from Allah's command to His servants.
The refusal to follow a warner does not clarify the selected heirs or their three conditions.
Explicitly depicts believers hastening in good deeds and being foremost in them.
The shared description of faithful servants is too general to clarify selection or inheritance.
The unchanging divine pattern offers no specific relation to the focus's inherited Book or rankings.
Uses inheritance in a prophetic household, supporting an inheritance broader than private material possession.
Repeats the exact phrase self-wronging and portrays its concrete moral posture in the garden owner's presumption.
The immediate sequel praises Allah for removing sorrow from those receiving the promised outcome.
Directly describes a community as moderate amid others whose deeds are evil.
Pairs wrongdoers with believers in gardens and names Allah's great bounty, but not Book inheritance.
The immediate sequel attributes permanent dwelling to Allah's bounty, explaining the focus's great bounty.
Distinguishes what Allah and His messenger give from Allah's future bounty, clarifying bounty as sourced in Allah.
Calls Paradise an inheritance granted to God's servants according to their guarded devotion.
Shows a Book given to Moses and later inherited amid doubt and dispute, a warning that transmission need not ensure reception.
The root for moderation frames a directed, upright way, but does not itself classify Book heirs.
The repeated qualification by Allah's permission is relevant but occurs in the distinct matter of prophetic signs.
Nearby condemnation of arrogant plotting contrasts with the focus's chosen servants but adds no direct connection.
Its rhetorical use of choosing exposes false claims of privileged selection and contrasts with Allah's actual choosing.
Explicitly speaks of people inheriting the Book yet remaining in troubling doubt and division.
Pharaoh's transgression supplies only a remote instance of wrongdoing.
Promises that Allah may enrich believers from His bounty, confirming bounty as a divine gift rather than earned possession.
Directly characterizes selected servants, though its distinctive criterion is remembrance of the final abode.
The immediate continuation presents the gardens entered by the heirs, extending the focus's promised bounty.
Repeatedly makes Jesus' acts contingent on Allah's permission, supporting the focus's qualification of precedence by permission.
Speech occurring only by permission is a distant analogue to action occurring by Allah's permission.
The passage of prior patterns does not clarify selection, inheritance, or the three recipient conditions.
It concerns a false claim about divine selection, offering only a polemical contrast to genuine choosing.
Wisdom given to Luqman leads to gratitude, a relevant model of receiving a divine gift responsibly.
The nearby contrast between darkness and light is too general to assess the focus's inheritance categories.
The proposed link treats ignorance too abstractly and does not bear on the focus's stated relations.
Solomon's inheritance from David supports inherited, divinely granted capacity rather than merely private estate.
Questions whether rapidly supplied wealth is truly good, qualifying simplistic readings of divine favor.
Defines the great bounty as Allah's gift to whom He wills, closely echoing the focus's closing clause.
Directly praises Allah and invokes His selected servants, closely paralleling divine choosing from among servants.
The nearby contrast of shade and heat does not develop the selected heirs or their graded response.
The lexical idea of going ahead is present, but the oath sequence does not specify good deeds or human recipients.
Recitation of the Qur'an and self-directed guidance offer a relevant but less direct account of receiving revelation.
Divine counting of all beings does not clarify Book inheritance or moral gradation.
A ruler uses ability supplied by his Lord, but the construction project is distant from inherited revelation.
States that Allah singles out whom He wills for mercy and possesses great bounty.
The nearby appeal of wrongdoers to act rightly supplies an eschatological contrast to the focus's self-wronging category.
Uses Allah's choosing in a doctrinal rebuttal, confirming choosing as divine initiative rather than lineage.
Directly identifies a ranked divine gift as bounty from Allah and calls it great.
The vision and cursed tree trial do not elucidate the focus's Book, selection, or recipient classes.
Explicitly denies divine wrongdoing and attributes wrong to the people themselves.
Treats an extraordinary gift as a test of gratitude, qualifying personal claims to divinely given ability.
Allah's increase in creation is a broad nearby expression of divine generosity, not inherited Book stewardship.
Again denies divine wrongdoing toward servants, supporting the focus's category of self-wronging.
Combines wrongdoing against oneself with the condition that a messenger is obeyed only by Allah's permission.
A messenger sent from within a people does not clarify the focus's selected heirs or their degrees.
The rejected proposal extends wrongdoing beyond the verse's stated comparison without a focused connection.
The affirmation of divine truth and greatness has no specific relation to Book inheritance or moral gradation.
The nearby deferral of consequence for human deeds gives only a broad context for wrongdoers.
The rejected imagery does not arise from the verse's denunciation of fabricated lies and denial.
The great triumph of believing doers broadly resembles promised reward but lacks the focus's inheritance and gradation.
Its use of precedence concerns fixed communal terms, not precedence in good deeds.
Ranks enduring righteous deeds above worldly wealth and children, resonating with precedence in good deeds.
The declaration of divine truth and exaltation does not materially connect to the focus's themes.
Believers' increased faith and submission after trial is only a broad model of faithful response.
Revealed clear signs bring servants from darkness to light, a relevant account of the Book's beneficent effect.
Mentions people of the Book, a request for a heavenly book, and wrongdoing, but not inheriting it well.
Divinely bestowed tranquility increasing faith is a general gift-response parallel, not Book inheritance.
Contrasts entry into mercy with punishment for wrongdoers, without the focus's threefold recipient structure.
Divine knowledge of unseen and seen does not specifically develop selection, inheritance, or good deeds.
Recording a speaker's claim and extending punishment offers no meaningful connection to the focus.
Allah's choosing of the religion for a family makes inherited commitment an ongoing responsibility, not a finished status.
Allah's permission and testing distinguish a faithful remnant, but the setting remains a military trial.
Calls the months part of Allah's Book and forbids people to wrong themselves, joining two focus motifs indirectly.
Sets a lasting garden and divine pleasure above worldly attractions for the God-conscious, a reward parallel to great bounty.
Explicitly describes Paradise as an inheritance after divine guidance and purified relations among its recipients.
Its appeal to remember bounty and act generously concerns a legal settlement rather than inherited revelation.
The haste is toward disbelief and the setting concerns distortion, offering an inverse of hastening in good deeds.
The rejected environmental association is not supported by the verse's concise judgment of wrongdoing.
Calls the revealed scripture guidance and mercy for those who do good, supporting differentiated fruitful reception.
Allah grants differentiated rank among prophets and gives David a scripture, a partial parallel to chosen bearers and a Book.
Allah's mercy and bringing believers from darkness to light parallels divine care for receptive servants.
Its failed attempt to race on the path without sight is a negative, figurative counterpart to rightly preceding in good.
The certainty of death and return for account does not clarify the focus's inheritance or recipient classes.
Links Allah's ultimate inheritance with differing ranks among those who spend and strive, closely matching inheritance and graded response.
Those given the Book who recite it as it should be recited provide a direct positive model of faithfully receiving inherited scripture.
The prayer that a messenger teach the Book and wisdom frames revelation as a divinely conferred, formative trust.
Connects recitation, purification, and teaching of the Book and wisdom, clarifying the Book's intended effect on its recipients.
Talut's selection by Allah despite social objection illuminates choosing as divine designation rather than inherited status or wealth.
Wisdom given to whom Allah wills is called abundant good, a close gift-and-bounty parallel to the focus.
Explicitly locates bounty in Allah's hand and says He gives it to whom He wills.
Links the Book and wisdom to becoming devoted servants of God, a relevant model for bearers of scripture.
Describes Allah's favor in sending a messenger to recite, purify, and teach the Book and wisdom.
Records the covenant imposed on those given the Book to make it clear rather than conceal it, directly qualifying inherited-scripture responsibility.
States that Allah gave Abraham's family the Book and wisdom along with a great kingdom, directly joining chosen lineage and scripture.
Describes Allah's favor in sending down the Book and wisdom and teaching what was previously unknown.
Presents a Book from Allah as light and clarification, relevant to the beneficent purpose of inherited revelation.
Calls the Torah guidance and light and identifies those charged with guarding Allah's Book, a direct custodial parallel.
Names the people to whom Allah gave the Book, judgment, and prophethood, closely paralleling selected recipients of scripture.
Calls the Qur'an a blessed Book sent down for people to follow, directly framing revelation as a received divine gift.
Moses receives written tablets containing instruction and explanation, an important instance of divine scriptural bestowal.
Explicitly says a later generation inherited the Book while taking fleeting worldly gain, a central warning against assuming inheritance ensures fidelity.
Commands rejoicing in Allah's bounty and mercy, identifying them as better than accumulated possessions.
Shows Moses' Book becoming an object of later dispute, complementing the focus's concern with differing responses to scripture.
Describes a revealed Arabic judgment and warns against following desires after knowledge, relevant to responsible reception of revelation.
Introduces a Book sent down to bring people from darkness into light, a direct account of scripture's guiding function.
States that the Qur'an guides to what is most upright and announces good news for those doing righteous deeds.
Commands recitation of the Book revealed from the Lord and affirms the unchangeability of His words.
Allah makes leaders who guide by His command and inspires them to perform good deeds, linking divine selection with enacted goodness.
Explicitly says that righteous servants will inherit the earth, giving a major inheritance-to-servants parallel.
Allah grants Abraham's line prophethood and the Book, directly connecting chosen descendants with transmitted scripture.
Commands recitation of the revealed Book and links it to prayer and moral restraint, clarifying its responsible use.
Moses receives the Book, which Allah makes guidance for Israel, a close precedent for a divinely transmitted Book among a people.
Those given knowledge recognize the Book sent down as truth that guides to the Mighty and Praiseworthy path.
Describes Allah as sending down the best discourse as a Book whose reception moves and softens receptive hearts.
Explicitly says Allah gave Moses guidance and made the Children of Israel inherit the Book.
Describes the Book as exalted and wise with Allah, reinforcing its divine, non-human origin.
Says Allah gave the Children of Israel the Book, judgment, and prophethood, then favored them over peoples.
Links the sending of messengers and the Book with justice, clarifying the social responsibility embedded in received revelation.
Places prophethood and the Book among Noah and Abraham's descendants, a direct lineage-and-scripture parallel.
Promises believers from the People of the Book a double share of mercy and says bounty belongs to Allah to give as He wills.
Describes the messenger's recitation, purification, and teaching of the Book and wisdom among his people.
Critiques those charged with the Torah who fail to carry it, a strong negative analogue to unfulfilled scriptural inheritance.
Names a messenger reciting purified scriptures, relevant to the mediated delivery of divine writing.
